figures.caption: Fig. 1: Comparison between prior training paradigms of deep matting and our self-supervised matting paradigm. Prior paradigms require large-scale dense annotations, while we can train an automatic matting model with only RGB images.

Fig. 4: LDDC accumulates textures during training. LDDC denotes the output of alpha-free matting, the estimated fixed point denotes the converged solution, and Lt denotes supervising alpha-free matting with Lt.

Fig. 5: Qualitative automatic results on AM-2K and P3M-NP-500. Our method produces better alpha mattes than AFM at details and recognizing foregrounds, and occasionally produces alpha mattes that are more plausible than ground truths.

Table 1: Automatic matting results. ∗ denotes that the backbone is initialized with DINOv2, and † denotes that a trimap-guided crop is applied to ensure the image patches contain unknown regions. Best performances and second performances of nonfull supervision are in boldface and underline, respectively.
Table 3: Scaling study on training data volume. Our method shows consistent performance gains with data volume increase.

Fig. 2: Technical pipeline of our self-supervised automatic image matting. We mine a prompt from frozen DINO to anchor semantics for subsequent matting, and utilize the alpha-RGB consistency to refine details.

Fig. 6: Qualitative results of ablations on (a) Mining semantic matting prompt, and (b) Detail matting. SMP is short for semantic matting prompt. Lseed produces a noisy foreground cue, while Lsea provides a more sound semantic matting prompt. LDDC forces image textures in boundaries, while Lt encourages a hard segmentation. Only by combining LDDC and Lt together produces optimal alpha mattes.

Fig. 3: Details of the proposed Semantic Inducer and Lsea. Lsea encourages similar patch nodes to have similar response values in the predicted semantic matting prompt. We supervise a cross attention layer to obtain the semantic matting prompt.
